topics.name: Diodes
topics.kicker: One-way valves for electric current · Turn AC into DC
topics.dates: First vacuum-tube version by John Ambrose Fleming, 1904
topics.briefing: A diode is an electronic part that lets electric current flow in only one direction, like a one-way valve for electricity. Most diodes today are made by joining two kinds of silicon, called p-type and n-type, and they are used to turn the alternating current from a wall outlet into the direct current that electronics need. Light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, are diodes that glow when current passes through them.
topics.answerHtml: diodes (accept diode; prompt on rectifiers or p-n junctions; do not accept “LEDs” or “transistors”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1904, John Ambrose Fleming built an early version of these devices from a vacuum tube, calling it an “oscillation valve,” to detect radio signals for Guglielmo Marconi’s wireless company. Modern versions of these devices are usually made from silicon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that let electric current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: Lee de Forest added a third electrode, a wire grid, to the vacuum-tube type of these devices, creating the Audion, which could amplify signals. Early crystal radio sets used a crude type of these devices called a “cat’s whisker,” a thin wire touching a crystal of galena.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these two-terminal parts that act as one-way valves for electric current.

tossups.p: In 1874, Karl Ferdinand Braun [“BROWN”] found that a metal point touching certain crystals could rectify electricity, the first semiconductor example of these devices. Modern examples of these devices are made at a junction between p-type and n-type silicon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that let current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: Zener [“ZEE-ner”] types of these devices, named for Clarence Zener, are designed to conduct backward once a set breakdown voltage is reached, so they can hold a voltage steady. When an ordinary one of these devices is reverse biased, it blocks nearly all flow.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components, made from p-n junctions, that pass current in just one direction.

tossups.p: Leo Esaki [“eh-SAH-kee”] shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics after inventing a “tunnel” type of these devices, in which the current drops as the voltage rises over a certain range. Ordinary types of these devices are called “non-ohmic,” since their current does not grow in proportion to the voltage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic parts, used as rectifiers, that let current flow only one way.

tossups.p: Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, and Shuji Nakamura won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for making efficient blue light-emitting versions of these devices, which made bright, energy-saving white lighting possible. In 1962, Nick Holonyak Jr. made the first practical light-emitting one that gave off visible red light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that let current pass in only one direction.

tossups.p: Four of these devices arranged in a diamond-shaped bridge make a full-wave rectifier, which flips the backward half of each cycle of alternating current so that both halves come out flowing the same way. A single one of these devices instead blocks every backward half-cycle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components that change AC into DC by letting current flow in just one direction.

tossups.p: Schottky [“SHOT-kee”] types of these devices join a metal directly to a semiconductor, which lets them switch on with less voltage than usual. On a circuit diagram, one of these devices is drawn as a triangle pointing at a short bar.
tossups.r: A painted stripe marks its cathode end. For 10 points, name these components that let current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: A silicon one of these devices needs about 0.7 volts across it in the forward direction before it conducts well. That happens when its p side is connected to the positive side of a battery, a setup called forward bias.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components, used as rectifiers, that block current flowing the wrong way.

tossups.p: At the heart of most of these devices is a thin depletion region, where electrons from the n-type side have filled the “holes” on the p-type side. That region acts as a barrier that only a large enough forward voltage can push current across.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic parts, used in rectifiers, that let current flow just one way.

tossups.p: A solar cell is basically a large, flat version of these devices: light striking its p-n junction knocks electrons loose and drives them around a circuit. Light-emitting versions of these devices do the reverse, giving off light when electrons cross the junction and fill holes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components, which pass current in only one direction and can turn AC into DC.

tossups.p: Blu-ray players read discs using a laser type of these devices that gives off blue-violet light, while CD players use a type that gives off infrared light. Other types of these devices glow in many colors in traffic lights and screens.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that let current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: Varactor [“vuh-RAK-ter”] types of these devices behave like capacitors whose value changes with the voltage across them, so they can tune radios without moving parts. Placing an ordinary one of these devices in line with a battery holder protects a gadget if the batteries go in backward.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components, often marked with a stripe, that let current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: In the early 1880s, Thomas Edison noticed that a heated filament inside a light bulb sent electricity across the vacuum to a nearby metal plate, but only when the plate was connected to the positive side. That “Edison effect” is the basis of vacuum-tube types of these devices.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components that let electric current flow in only one direction.

tossups.p: A TV remote control flashes coded pulses of infrared light from a light-emitting type of these devices, and the TV picks them up with a light-sensitive type of these devices. Both types are built around a junction of p-type and n-type material.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these components that let current flow in only one direction, often used as rectifiers.

trap.title: The device, not LEDs
trap.body: Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) are just one kind of this device, so this page does not accept “LED” or “light-emitting diode” when a tossup is about the general one-way part. Players also confuse it with the transistor, which usually has three terminals and can amplify or switch signals, and with the triode, the three-electrode vacuum tube that Lee de Forest made by adding a grid. Saying “rectifier” earns only a prompt, since that word names the job, not the part.
trap.fix: One-way flow, AC to DC, p-n junctions, anode and cathode, Fleming’s valve, and Zener types mean diodes. Three terminals, amplifying, and switching mean transistors. If a question asks specifically for the devices that give off light, then answer “LEDs.”
trap.line: Real answer line: diodes (accept diode; prompt on rectifiers or p-n junctions; do not accept “LEDs” or “transistors”)

topics.name: Ampère’s law
topics.kicker: Magnetic fields from electric currents · One of Maxwell’s equations
topics.dates: Named for André-Marie Ampère; corrected by Maxwell in the early 1860s
topics.briefing: Ampère’s law says that if you add up the magnetic field all the way around any closed loop, you get a number set by the electric current passing through that loop. Physicists use it to find the magnetic field around a straight wire or inside a coil without hard calculations. James Clerk Maxwell later added a missing piece, and the corrected law became one of the four Maxwell’s equations that describe electricity, magnetism, and light.
topics.answerHtml: Ampère’s law (accept Ampère’s circuital law or Ampère–Maxwell law; prompt on Ampère or Maxwell’s equations; do not accept “Biot–Savart law” or “Faraday’s law”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This law gives the wrong answer in the gap of a charging capacitor unless it includes a “displacement current” term, which James Clerk Maxwell added in the early 1860s. With that term, a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, just as a current does.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through the loop.

tossups.p: Using this law with a circular path around a long, straight wire shows that the wire’s magnetic field falls off as one over the distance from the wire. This law plays the same role for magnetism that Gauss’s law plays for electricity, making problems with lots of symmetry easy.
tossups.r: It is applied by drawing an imaginary closed loop around a current. For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations.

tossups.p: Inside a doughnut-shaped coil called a toroid, this law shows that the magnetic field weakens with distance from the doughnut’s center, while outside the coil the field is zero. This law also gives the nearly uniform field inside a long, straight coil called a solenoid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that links a magnetic field to the electric current that makes it.

tossups.p: Outside a coaxial cable whose inner wire and outer sleeve carry equal currents in opposite directions, this law predicts no magnetic field at all, since no net current passes through a loop drawn around the cable. When using this law, only the current that passes through the chosen closed path counts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around any closed loop to the current through it.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell called this law’s namesake “the Newton of electricity.” That namesake began his experiments in 1820, within weeks of learning that Hans Christian Ørsted had made a compass needle swing using a current.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, named for a French physicist, about the magnetic field produced by electric currents.

tossups.p: The original form of this law works only for steady currents that do not change over time. Maxwell’s corrected version of this law, together with Faraday’s law of induction, predicted waves of electric and magnetic fields traveling at the speed of light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, which says that electric currents produce magnetic fields that circle around them.

tossups.p: The Biot–Savart [“bee-OH suh-VAR”] law gives the same answers as this law, but this law is far easier to use when a problem has a lot of symmetry. The constant in this law, mu-naught, is called the permeability of free space.
tossups.r: This law says that the magnetic field added up around a closed loop is proportional to the current through it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law contains the constant mu-naught, the permeability of free space, which is about four pi times ten to the negative seventh in SI units. That constant multiplies the current that passes through the closed path in this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that links the magnetic field around a loop to the current through it, one of Maxwell’s four equations.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake called his new field of study “electrodynamics.” When using this law around a wire, a right-hand rule gives the direction of the magnetic field: point your thumb along the current, and your fingers curl the way the field circles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, about the magnetic fields made by currents.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake also showed in 1820 that two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other, a result described by a separate “force law” named for him. James Clerk Maxwell later added a displacement current term to this law.
tossups.r: This law relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current inside it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake, one of 72 scientists whose names are engraved on the Eiffel Tower, was largely self-taught and became a professor at the École Polytechnique [“ay-KOHL po-lee-tek-NEEK”] in Paris. Maxwell’s corrected version of this law is one of his four famous equations.
tossups.r: This law relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current passing through it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law shows that the magnetic field just outside a long, tightly wound solenoid is nearly zero, while inside it equals mu-naught times the number of turns per meter times the current. It works easily around a straight wire, where the field is equally strong all the way around a circle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that links a magnetic field to the current that makes it.

tossups.p: Faraday’s law says that a changing magnetic field makes an electric field, while the corrected form of this law says that a changing electric field makes a magnetic field. That pairing led James Clerk Maxwell to predict that light is an electromagnetic wave.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current through the loop.

tossups.p: Applying this law inside a thick wire with current spread evenly across it shows that the magnetic field grows in proportion to the distance from the wire’s center, then weakens outside the wire. The magnetic field lines around the wire form closed circles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that relates a magnetic field to the electric current producing it.

tossups.p: The left side of this law adds up the magnetic field all the way around a closed path, a quantity called the field’s circulation. This law’s namesake proposed that tiny loops of current inside magnets cause their magnetism.
tossups.r: The right side of this law is mu-naught times the current through the path. For 10 points, name this law.

clues.t: Relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through the loop

Gives the nearly uniform field inside a long solenoid (mu-naught × turns per meter × current); just outside, the field is nearly zero
Applied by drawing an imaginary closed path, often a circle around a wire, and adding up the magnetic field along it
Plays the same role for magnetism that Gauss’s law plays for electricity, making symmetric problems easy
Right-hand rule: point your thumb along the current, and your fingers curl the way the magnetic field circles
Its constant is mu-naught, the permeability of free space, about 4π × 10⁻⁷ in SI units
Gives the same fields as the Biot–Savart law but is much easier to use when a problem has lots of symmetry
Inside a doughnut-shaped toroid coil, the field weakens with distance from the center; outside the coil, it is zero
Outside a coaxial cable carrying equal and opposite currents, it predicts no magnetic field at all
Inside a thick wire with evenly spread current, the field grows in proportion to the distance from the center
Its original form works only for steady currents that do not change over time
James Clerk Maxwell called its namesake “the Newton of electricity”
Its namesake began his experiments in 1820, within weeks of learning of Hans Christian Ørsted’s compass-needle discovery
Its namesake called his new field of study “electrodynamics”
Its namesake showed in 1820 that parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract, described by a separate force law
Its namesake is one of 72 scientists whose names are engraved on the Eiffel Tower
Its namesake was largely self-taught and became a professor at the École Polytechnique in Paris
Its namesake proposed that tiny loops of current inside magnets cause their magnetism
Its left side, the magnetic field added up all the way around a closed path, is called the field’s circulation

trap.title: Which electromagnetism law?
trap.body: Several laws of electricity and magnetism show up together. This law links the magnetic field circling a closed loop to the current passing through it; Gauss’s law links the electric field through a closed surface to the charge inside; Faraday’s law says a changing magnetic field makes a voltage; and the Biot–Savart law builds up a magnetic field piece by piece. The same French physicist also has a separate force law about parallel wires, and the unit of current carries his name, so saying just “Ampère” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Closed loops (Amperian loops), the current enclosed, solenoids, toroids, and Maxwell’s displacement current mean this law. Closed surfaces and enclosed charge mean Gauss’s law; induction, generators, and Lenz’s law mean Faraday’s law; adding up the field from tiny pieces of wire means the Biot–Savart law.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ampère’s law (accept Ampère’s circuital law or Ampère–Maxwell law; prompt on Ampère or Maxwell’s equations; do not accept “Biot–Savart law” or “Faraday’s law”)

topics.name: Spin (physics)
topics.kicker: A particle’s built-in angular momentum · Up or down for electrons
topics.briefing: Spin is a built-in amount of angular momentum that electrons, protons, and many other particles carry, as if they were tiny spinning tops, though nothing is actually turning. An electron’s spin can point only “up” or “down,” and spin makes electrons and protons act like tiny magnets: lined-up electron spins make permanent magnets, and MRI scanners flip the spins of hydrogen nuclei. Particles with half-integer spin (like 1/2 or 3/2) are called fermions, and those with whole-number spin are called bosons.
topics.answerHtml: spin (accept spin angular momentum, intrinsic angular momentum, or spin quantum number; prompt on angular momentum)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ralph Kronig thought of this property early in 1925 but did not publish it after Wolfgang Pauli criticized the idea. Later that year, George Uhlenbeck [“OO-len-bek”] and Samuel Goudsmit [“GOWD-smit”] proposed it to explain why some spectral lines split into close pairs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles, which for an electron can point only up or down.

tossups.p: Hendrik Lorentz objected that if this property came from an electron actually turning, the electron’s surface would have to move faster than light. In 1928, Paul Dirac’s equation for the electron produced this property automatically.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, a built-in angular momentum that equals one-half for electrons.

tossups.p: In 1922, Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach [“GAIR-lahk”] fired silver atoms through an uneven magnetic field and saw the beam split into two parts, a result later explained by this property of each atom’s outermost electron. For an electron, this property can take only two values.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles, often described as “up” or “down.”

tossups.p: Wolfgang Pauli proved in 1940 that this property decides whether a particle obeys his exclusion principle. Particles with half-integer values of this property, such as electrons, are called fermions, while those with whole-number values, such as photons, are called bosons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum carried by particles such as electrons and protons.

tossups.p: A particle with a value of one-half for this property must be rotated a full 720 degrees, not just 360, before its wavefunction returns to exactly its original value. Electrons have that value of this property, which makes each electron act like a tiny magnet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, a particle’s built-in angular momentum, which is up or down for an electron.

tossups.p: Albert Fert and Peter Grünberg [“GROON-bairk”] won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering giant magnetoresistance, which depends on this property of electrons and let hard drives store far more data. In iron magnets, this property of many unpaired electrons lines up in small regions called domains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles, which for an electron is one-half.

tossups.p: Chemists identify molecules with NMR spectroscopy, which detects atomic nuclei that have this property. MRI scanners line up this property of hydrogen nuclei in the body with a powerful magnet, then flip it with pulses of radio waves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles such as protons and electrons.

tossups.p: Hydrogen atoms in space give off radio waves 21 centimeters long when the electron flips this property to point the opposite way from the proton’s. Astronomers use that 21-centimeter line to map the spiral arms of the Milky Way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, a built-in angular momentum that makes particles act like tiny magnets.

tossups.p: Atoms of helium-4 have a total of zero for this property, so they act as bosons, which lets liquid helium-4 flow without any friction as a superfluid at very low temperatures. Atoms of helium-3 have a total of one-half and act as fermions instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, a particle’s built-in angular momentum, that is up or down for an electron.

tossups.p: This property explained the “anomalous” Zeeman effect, in which spectral lines split into unexpected patterns in a magnetic field. It is described by the fourth quantum number, which is either plus one-half or minus one-half.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, a particle’s built-in angular momentum, which makes each electron act like a tiny magnet.

tossups.p: Before this property was named, Wolfgang Pauli described a mysterious “two-valuedness” of the electron that classical physics could not explain. The Pauli exclusion principle says that two electrons sharing an orbital must have opposite values of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, which can be “up” or “down” for an electron.

tossups.p: The hypothetical graviton would have a value of two for this property, and the Higgs boson is the only known elementary particle with a value of zero. Photons and gluons each have a value of one for this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, a built-in angular momentum that is one-half for electrons.

tossups.p: This property is measured in units of h-bar, which is Planck’s constant divided by two pi, and an electron carries exactly one-half of a unit. In orbital diagrams, this property is shown by drawing each electron as an arrow pointing up or down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum carried by electrons, protons, and neutrons.

tossups.p: In the Einstein–de Haas effect, magnetizing a hanging iron cylinder makes it start to rotate, because lining up its electrons’ magnetism also lines up this property, and the total angular momentum must stay the same. Particles called fermions have half-integer values of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this built-in angular momentum of particles, which is up or down for an electron.

tossups.p: Liquid oxygen clings between the poles of a strong magnet because each oxygen molecule has two unpaired electrons with matching values of this property. Hund’s rule says that electrons fill orbitals of equal energy one at a time, all with the same value of this property, before any of them pair up.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantum property, a built-in angular momentum that is “up” or “down” for an electron.

clues.t: A particle’s own built-in angular momentum, carried by electrons, protons, and neutrons even though nothing is actually rotating
For an electron it equals one-half and can point only “up” or “down”
Particles with half-integer values are fermions (like electrons); particles with whole-number values are bosons (like photons)
MRI scanners line up this property of hydrogen nuclei with a strong magnet and flip it with radio waves to make images

Photons and gluons have a value of one; the Higgs boson is the only known elementary particle with a value of zero
Hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio line comes from the electron flipping it to point opposite the proton’s; it maps the Milky Way’s spiral arms
In orbital diagrams it is shown by drawing each electron as an arrow pointing up or down
Hund’s rule: electrons fill equal-energy orbitals one at a time with matching values before any pair up
Ralph Kronig thought of it first, early in 1925, but did not publish after Wolfgang Pauli criticized the idea
Hendrik Lorentz objected that a literally rotating electron’s surface would have to move faster than light
Paul Dirac’s 1928 equation for the electron produced it automatically
Pauli proved in 1940 that it decides whether a particle obeys his exclusion principle (fermions do; bosons do not)
A particle with a value of one-half must be rotated 720 degrees, not 360, before its wavefunction returns to its original value
Giant magnetoresistance, which depends on it and let hard drives store far more data, won Albert Fert and Peter Grünberg the 2007 Nobel Prize
Before it was named, Wolfgang Pauli described a mysterious “two-valuedness” of the electron that classical physics could not explain
Helium-4 atoms have a total of zero and act as bosons, so liquid helium-4 can flow without friction as a superfluid; helium-3 atoms are fermions
It explained the “anomalous” Zeeman effect, in which spectral lines split into unexpected patterns in a magnetic field
The hypothetical graviton would have a value of two
Measured in units of h-bar (Planck’s constant divided by 2π); an electron carries one-half of a unit
Einstein–de Haas effect: magnetizing a hanging iron cylinder makes it rotate, because lining up its electrons’ magnetism also lines up this property
Liquid oxygen clings to a strong magnet because each oxygen molecule has two unpaired electrons with matching values
NMR spectroscopy identifies molecules by detecting atomic nuclei that have this property

trap.title: Spin or angular momentum?
trap.body: This property is a particle’s built-in angular momentum, so plain “angular momentum” earns only a prompt here, while the angular momentum page does not accept “spin.” An electron also has orbital angular momentum from moving around the nucleus, which is a different thing, and “magnetic moment” names the tiny magnet that this property creates. Stern–Gerlach and Pauli exclusion clues can also lure a wrong buzz of “electrons” when the question asks for the property.
trap.fix: Up or down, one-half, fermions and bosons, Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, the Stern–Gerlach split, MRI, and the 21-centimeter line mean spin. If the giveaway asks for “these particles,” say electrons; if it asks for the rule that two electrons in one orbital must be opposite, say the Pauli exclusion principle.
trap.line: Real answer line: spin (accept spin angular momentum, intrinsic angular momentum, or spin quantum number; prompt on angular momentum)
